FirstIntroduction: ^Oh hey, this is rare. Looks like I got a visitor today!
^I'm Suzy. I'm in charge of everything graphical you see on screen: Sprites, colours, collisions, movement...
^To handle them I have to move fast. 16MHz fast, actually! That's four times faster than Mikey, which comes in handy when you're pushing pixels like I do!
ReturningIntroduction: ^> Could you explain your role here again?
^> Mind if I have another go at 'Collision Control'?

c-1: ^Love your enthusiasm! Need a quick refresher?

Questions: ^> Do you have any unique tricks for processing graphics?
^> Any chance I could see you in action?

c-0: ^Okay, picture this: You want a spaceship zooming across the screen. You don't just throw me an image and say "go". I need two things:
^2. A Sprite Control Block - basically a set of instructions telling me how to handle it.
^Give me those, and I'll blit that thing onto the screen buffer in no time.
c-1: ^Ah, my secret sauce! I have a technique that no other consoles at my time have figured out.
^While I'm drawing, I also keep an eye out for overlaps. Each sprite gets a collision number - sort of like a nametag, numbered 0 to 15.

^If two sprites overlap, I record the highest number into something called the collision depository. You (or your game code) can check it afterward to see what hit what. And yes - this is pixel-perfect. None of that rectangle-guessing nonsense other consoles are used to.
c-2: ^Absolutely! I'm actually really well known for reusing graphics to be more efficient, I'm super proud of it.

^One piece of pixel data - let's say a robot - can be reused in multiple SCBs. I can draw it in different spots, scales, or colours without duplicating the actual image data. Saves memory and still looks great, Win-win!
c-3: ^I can do you one better! I'll let you try your hand at 'Collision Control'!

CollisionControlInstructions: ^Just press the Spacebar whenever you see two objects collide on-screen.
^Sounds simple but its quite tough! You sure you're ready?

c-0: ^I love your confidence, Let's get started!
c-1: ^In the meantime, make sure you meet Mikey if you haven't already.

b: ^That task can get really hectic at times but you held your own pretty well.
^Here, take this 'Collision Control' badge as a token of my appreciation!
^Tough isn't it? Would you like to try again?

c-1: ^Feel free to come back and try again whenever you'd like.

FirstIntroduction: ^Hi there, I am Mikey, very pleased to meet you.
^Unlike my partner Suzy you may not see what I do, but you'd notice pretty fast if I stopped doing it.

^I manage the game's logic, handle inputs, sound, as well as keeping Suzy on schedule. I run at 4 MHz - not flashy, but reliable. Suzy jokes that I'm slow, and she's not wrong. But I get a lot done with each cycle.
ReturningIntroduction: ^Oh, you're back. Wanna give me a hand?
^> Could I ask you a question?
^> Yeah, what do you need me to do?

c-1: ^We're doing 'Byte Runner', do you know it?

Questions: ^> How does an 8-bit CPU like you work?
^> What kind of sound can you make?
^> Anything I can help you with?

c-0: ^I'm based on the 6502 family of processors. Classic architecture. I handle 8 bits of data at a time- meaning I process numbers from 0 to 255 in a single operation.
^Larger numbers? More complex math? I break them down and handle them step by step. It's slower, sure, but it works. No floating point, no shortcuts. Just pure byte-by-byte logic.
^I operate within a 16-bit address space, which gives me 64 kilobytes of memory. That's the total memory I can access at once - for code, variables, assets, everything.

^It sounds small by today's standards, but with proper structure and clever loading, it's enough. And we were the pioneers of our time. Suzy, for instance, knows how to reuse graphics. I myself also admire that efficiency.
c-1: ^I control a 4-channel sound system. Each channel plays its own waveform - like square waves, sawtooth, or noise.

^You set the pitch, volume, and length, and I handle the playback. I can even mix in digital samples, though that's more demanding. I'm no synthesizer, but I do a good job delivering clean, retro audio.
c-2: ^I work closely with Suzy, handling video timing - starting the screen refresh cycle, managing blanking intervals, and making sure Suzy doesn't draw mid-frame.
^If you've ever seen screen-tearing in a game, that's what happens when graphics and timing go out of sync. I make sure that never happens here.
^Although I handle a lot of tasks, handling anything more than one task at a time isn't my thing especially not how modern systems do. Don't get me wrong though I do move fast, so it feels smooth.
^I run a main loop, one task at a time: check input, update logic, refresh screen, repeat.
c-3: ^Sure, it would be nice to have another helping hand around here. Would you like to try and allocate some bytes for me, experience for yourself how an 8-bit processor works? Join me in 'Byte Runner'!

ByteRunnerInstructions: ^Don't worry it's simple, I'll send you address signals down the bus - you read 'em, and drag my byte workers into the right memory slots before Suzy hogs the line again!

c-1: ^No stress, come back whenever you're ready.
